nameStory: Purple-vein geranium gets its name from the distinctive purple veins that often run through its bright blue petals, creating a beautiful striped pattern. The scientific name wallichianum honors Dr. Nathaniel Wallich, a Danish plant hunter who explored the Himalayas in the early 1800s. Despite its common name suggesting purple flowers, this geranium actually blooms in shades of blue with those telltale darker veins.
description: Purple-vein geranium is a low-growing perennial flower that forms spreading mounds about 2 feet tall and wide. This hardy plant produces masses of bright blue, five-petaled flowers throughout the summer months, often with darker purple veins creating a striking pattern. Originally from the high mountains of the Himalayas, it has fuzzy, deeply-lobed leaves that feel soft to the touch. With only 2 recorded sightings in New England, this is an extremely rare garden escapee that most nature explorers will never encounter in the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright blue five-petaled flowers about an inch across, often with distinctive darker purple veins running through the petals like delicate watercolor brushstrokes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed, palm-shaped leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy due to fine hairs covering the surface, with toothed edges that give them a jagged appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mounds up to 2 feet tall and wide, with trailing stems that can sprawl across the ground or cascade over edges

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops the characteristic crane's-bill seed pods that split dramatically when ripe, flinging seeds away from the parent plant with an audible 'pop'

habitat: As an extremely rare garden escapee in New England, purple-vein geranium would most likely be found near old homesteads, abandoned gardens, or areas where landscaping waste was dumped. It prefers well-drained soil and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. Given its Himalayan origins, it might persist in cooler, mountainous areas of northern New England where conditions more closely match its native habitat.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, fuzzy rosettes of deeply-lobed leaves. Young foliage often has a fresh, green scent when crushed between fingers.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with masses of bright blue flowers appearing from June through August. The soft, hairy leaves are at their fullest and most distinctive.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in mild years. Seed pods mature and split open, launching seeds with small explosive pops that you can sometimes hear in quiet gardens.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in cold climates, leaving no above-ground parts visible. In milder areas, some basal leaves may persist through winter.

funFact: Purple-vein geranium's seed pods are natural catapults that can launch their seeds up to 15 feet away with enough force to make an audible popping sound - earning all plants in this family the nickname 'crane's-bills' for their long, beak-like seed pods that split and curl back like a startled bird's neck!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with wild geranium, New England's common native species, but wild geranium has pink or white flowers instead of blue. Remember: if you see bright blue geranium flowers with purple veins, you've likely found something very special and rare! Wild geranium also blooms earlier in spring while purple-vein geranium flowers through summer.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums (Geranium species) with the common red geraniums sold at garden centers, which are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like this one are also called 'crane's-bills' and are completely different plants that are hardy in New England winters, while pelargoniums must be brought indoors or treated as annuals.
compareHints: Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms. It's also larger and more robust than many of our native crane's-bills, with a distinctly spreading growth habit. The purple veining in the petals is particularly distinctive, as most other geranium species have solid-colored flowers or much subtler markings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
